newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Anarchy spreads in Albanian town after shootout.
newsitem.headline: Anarchy spreads in Albanian town after shootout.

text.p: Residents of this bleak southern Albanian port town mourned their dead on Saturday after a bloody night-time gun battle in which nine people were reported to have been killed.
Three protesters were shot dead during a two-hour-long exchange of gunfire between protesters and secret police.
The National Information Service, or the so-called Shik secret police said six of its men had been killed in the violence, three from gunshot wounds.
Reporters who visited the town mortuary found only four bodies -- the three protesters, including a 17-year-old and one Shik officer.

Hours after the shooting, residents awoke to the sound of scattered gunfire across the dilapidated town of 80,000 as scores of youths, armed with guns and automatic rifles, paraded through the dusty streets and fired live rounds into the air.
Uniformed police were nowhere to be seen.

Some 2,000 protesters, almost all of them carrying weapons, gathered outside the seafront university in the bright morning sun and observed one minute's silence for what they called the three martyrs of democracy.

The gunbattle occured at the local headquarters of the Shik, and was apparently sparked by a stabbing at the university were 42 students entered the 10th day of an anti-government hunger strike. The stabbing victim survived the attack.
Eyewitnesses said protesters, who had turned out in force to show their support for the students, pursued Shik officers after one of them was believed to have carried out the knifing.

The Shik headquarters were then set on fire. Part of the two-storey building was still burning on Saturday morning, and pools of blood could be seen on the floors where documents and papers lay scattered.

In a statement read out on Albanian state television, the secret police said two of its officers had died in the blaze, while another was beaten to death after being dragged out of the building by an angry mob.

After six weeks of mass protests against President Sali Berisha's right-wing government, sparked by the collapse of a string of dubious pyramid investment schemes in January, Vlore has residents appeared to have taken control of the town.
Vlore has long been considered a symbol of national pride. Albania's first government met in the town just after Albania became a nation in 1912 by splitting from the Ottoman empire.

Vlore is also known as the town of the national flag as the red banner showing a black two-headed eagle was first hoisted in the port on November 28, 1912, for the first time since national hero Skanderbeg ruled the territory in the 15th century.

While small childred gathered handfuls of spent cartridges in front of the university building, protest leaders declared five days of mourning for their killed comrades, whom they called martyrs of democracy.
"We proclaim five days of mourning and ask you to make sure no songs are sung, not even a weapon should be fired from this moment," student leader Luftar Petoshati said.

But his appeal to take weapons away from children appeared to fall on deaf ears. A 12-year old boy, clutching a tear-gas cannister, told reporters his friend was cruising through Vlore with a machinegun slung over his shoulder.

Regular police forces all but abandoned the town last month after an angry mob stoned a group of riot policemen, stripped them to their underwear and burnt their gear. One man was shot dead during the clash on February 10.
Residents say they now fear that the embattled government will send in the military to restore order.
Just north of Vlore, protesters blocked the country's main north-south road with trees and burnt-out cars in an apparent effort to prevent police or military reinforcements from reaching the town.
"Parliament has declared war on us, there's no more peace," said a local resident. "If the army comes in, thousands will be killed here."
